Can a squatter take a North Dakota house?

Rarely, and only after satisfying every element of the adverse possession statute for a long stretch of years. Under N.D.C.C. 47-06-03, title vests after ten years of actual, open, adverse and undisputed possession under color of title, and the possessor must also have paid every tax and assessment legally levied on the land.

A stranger who moves into a vacant house and stays a few months has no ownership claim at all. That person also risks criminal trespass charges, covered below. If you find someone living in your house, act early. Your strongest position is a record that shows you stayed in control of the property.

Ten-year and twenty-year rules

North Dakota runs two separate clocks. The ten-year rule in 47-06-03 applies when the possessor holds under color of title and has paid the taxes. The twenty-year periods in chapter 28-01 limit how long an owner has to sue to recover land and cover claims that lack the tax element.

StatuteRule
47-06-03Ten years of actual, open, adverse and undisputed possession under color of title, plus payment of all taxes and assessments
28-01-04A suit to recover real property is barred unless the plaintiff or a predecessor held possession within twenty years before the suit
28-01-07The holder of legal title is presumed to be in possession, and anyone else's occupation is presumed subordinate unless held adversely for twenty years
28-01-08An occupant under a written instrument, judgment or decree who occupies continuously for twenty years is deemed to hold adversely

Section 28-01-07 tilts toward the record owner. A squatter has to prove a long, unbroken occupation of the kind the law recognizes.

What counts as possession

The statute names particular acts, and the list changes depending on whether the occupant claims under a written document. With a written instrument, decree or judgment, land counts as possessed if it is usually cultivated or improved, protected by a substantial enclosure, or used to supply fuel or fencing timber. With no written instrument, only two of those count: a substantial enclosure, or usual cultivation or improvement. Section 28-01-10 adds that without a written instrument, only the premises actually occupied are deemed held adversely.

  • A house that sits empty and unfenced does not meet the enclosure or cultivation test on its own.
  • A contract for deed counts as color of title from the day it is executed.
  • A county that holds land under a tax deed is not treated as possessing it adversely.

Color of title means a document that looks like it passes ownership but is flawed. A defective deed, a decree of heirship and a contract for deed all qualify. A tenant who stays after a lease ends is a holdover, and the eviction statute handles that situation.

Chapin v. Letcher and the tax requirement

In Chapin v. Letcher, 93 N.W.2d 415, decided December 2, 1958, the North Dakota Supreme Court affirmed a judgment quieting title for people who relied on ten years of possession. The court treated a decree of heirship and deeds from heirs as color of title, and it let the claimants add the possession and tax payments of those who held before them.

It also ruled that a defendant's answer disputing title interrupts the ten years only if the defendant wins that claim. A denial that fails does not stop the clock. Fights over adverse possession tend to turn on paper, so an owner should hold on to tax receipts and any notice letters.

When staying in someone else's house is a crime

It can be a felony. Under N.D.C.C. 12.1-22-03, a person who knowingly enters or remains in a dwelling without license or privilege commits a class C felony. Unlawfully detaining, occupying or trespassing on a residential dwelling is a class C felony the first time and a class B felony for a repeat offense at the same dwelling.

  • Entering or remaining in a building without privilege is a class A misdemeanor.
  • Entering a place after notice against trespass, given directly or by posting, is a class B misdemeanor. Each sign must carry the name of the person posting it.
  • Staying on property after an authorized person asks you to leave is a class B misdemeanor.
  • A peace officer may instead cite a person for entering posted or fenced land as a noncriminal offense with a $250 fine.

To rely on the trespass statute, give a clear, documented request to leave and then call law enforcement.

Removing someone from your property

The owner files an eviction action in district court under chapter 47-32. Section 47-32-01 reaches entering by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth on another's prior actual possession and holding on to it, unlawfully keeping possession by force or threats, and staying after a foreclosure sale, deed or cancelled contract for deed once the redemption time has run.

In holdover, nonpayment, foreclosure-related and lease-violation cases, the landlord gives three days' written notice before filing. The summons sets an appearance date 3 to 15 days after it is issued, and a winning plaintiff receives a judgment for immediate restitution. The court may stay enforcement up to five days for substantial hardship, except where the case rests on disturbing the peace.

Nobody can be evicted without an order from a district court. The court's forms are not open to an LLC or corporation, which must be represented by a lawyer who practices in North Dakota. Do not change the locks or carry out belongings yourself. The Attorney General's guidance bars lockouts and taking a tenant's property.

Protecting a vacant house

Treat the house as property you must visibly control, and keep paperwork that proves it.

  • Inspect on a regular schedule and keep dated notes or photos.
  • Post no-trespassing signs carrying your name, and keep the structure secured.
  • Pay the property tax on time, because tax payment is one element a claimant must show.
  • Keep the deed, probate papers and tax statements together if the house is inherited.
  • Give a written request to leave to anyone found inside, then involve law enforcement and an attorney.

Tax records cut both ways. Notices go to the owner at the last-known address, so an inherited house whose notices reach a former owner can slide into delinquency unnoticed.

Selling with an unwanted occupant

An occupant adds work but does not block a sale. A buyer who purchases as-is takes the house with its problems, and a sale can move forward while you resolve the occupancy, provided the contract says how the property will be delivered. Tell the title company about any occupant early. The parties will want to know whether the person is a tenant, a family member or a trespasser.

The order of steps usually goes like this: document who is inside and when you found them, give the written request to leave, involve law enforcement or file the eviction action, and then set the closing date around the result. A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands and without a lender's inspection timeline can make that scheduling easier, since fewer outside parties have to see the property.

If you are unsure of an occupant's status, an attorney can sort that out. The statutes above are the starting point.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in North Dakota?

Ten years under 47-06-03, if the person has color of title and has paid all taxes and assessments on the land. Chapter 28-01 sets twenty-year periods for other cases.

Do squatters have rights in North Dakota?

Not automatically. The law presumes the record owner holds possession, and an occupant must prove every element of the statute. Entering or remaining in a dwelling without privilege can also be a class C felony.

Does a squatter have to pay taxes to claim a house?

Yes, under the ten-year rule. The possessor must have paid all taxes and assessments legally levied on the land.

Can I change the locks on someone living in my North Dakota house?

The Attorney General's guidance bars lockouts of tenants, so the safer route is the legal one. A person unlawfully in the house can be removed by court order in an eviction action or by law enforcement under the trespass statute.

What is color of title in North Dakota?

It is a written claim to the land, such as a deed, decree or contract for deed. A contract for deed counts as color of title from its execution.

Which rental rules apply when you sell

Four sets of rules matter most: the security deposit statute, the notice rules for ending a tenancy, the limits on landlord entry, and the eviction procedure. All of them sit in chapter 47-16 and chapter 47-32 of the North Dakota Century Code. If you plan to sell a house with a tenant in it, each of these has to be handled correctly, whether the buyer wants the tenant to stay or wants the house vacant.

This guide summarizes the statutes. It is general information and not legal advice, so a landlord with a dispute in progress should talk to a North Dakota attorney.

Security deposit rules

Under section 47-16-07.1, a landlord may generally collect a deposit of up to one month's rent, and must hold it in a federally insured, interest-bearing account for the tenant's benefit. The deductions and the return deadline are tightly set, and getting them wrong can cost a landlord triple the amount wrongly kept.

North Dakota security deposit rules
TopicRule
Deposit capOne month's rent, with exceptions for a tenant with a felony conviction or a prior judgment for violating a rental agreement
Pet depositNo more than the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent; not for service or companion animals
Return deadlineItemized deductions and any balance within 30 days after the lease ends and possession is delivered
InterestNot required if the tenant lived there less than nine months
Wrongful withholdingExposes the landlord to treble damages

Deductions may cover damage or unpaid rent but not normal wear and tear. A sale does not erase the deposit. Handle it in the closing paperwork, and ask your title company how the deposit and its interest will pass to the new owner.

The move-in condition statement

The landlord must give the tenant a written statement describing the property's facilities and condition when the rental agreement begins, and both parties sign it. Under N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.2 it serves as prima facie proof of the condition on that date.

Tenants should check the report before signing, because a tenant is presumed responsible for damage that is not listed. For a landlord preparing to sell, the signed statement is also the best record of what the house looked like when the tenant arrived. Keep a copy with the lease so a buyer and the title company can see it.

Showing the house to buyers

A landlord may enter at reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner for listed purposes, and showings to purchasers are among them. Section 47-16-07.3 also allows entry at any time in an emergency, or when the landlord reasonably believes the tenant has abandoned the unit or is in substantial violation of the lease.

  • Unless it is impractical, the landlord must notify the tenant and ask for consent that identifies a specific time.
  • Consent cannot be unreasonably withheld, and it is presumed if the tenant does not object after notice of a time certain.
  • Using access rights to harass or intimidate a tenant is prohibited.

Plan showings around the tenant's schedule and put the notice in writing. A string of unannounced visits can turn a cooperative tenant into a difficult one.

Ending a tenancy when the landlord sells

Selling a house does not by itself end a lease, so the way to end a tenancy depends on the type of tenancy. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended by either side with written notice of at least one calendar month, delivered on any day, and rent is owed through the termination date. For a tenancy with no stated term, notice must be at least as long as the lease period, up to one calendar month.

Changing the terms of a month-to-month tenancy takes written notice from the landlord at least 30 days before month's end, and the new terms apply if the tenant stays. A tenant who does not accept the change may end the tenancy at the end of the month with at least 25 days' notice.

A lease that requires notice longer than one month must say so and include a space for the tenant's initials. Without the initials, the tenant may end the tenancy on the last day of a month with one calendar month's notice.

What a landlord must keep in working order

The landlord's baseline duties are to meet building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, keep the unit fit to live in, and keep shared areas clean and safe. Section 47-16-13.1 also requires waste removal, running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, with listed exceptions, and the landlord gets a reasonable time to fix a problem after being told.

Tenants carry duties too under 47-16-13.2: keep their area clean and safe, dispose of waste, avoid damaging the premises, and avoid disturbing neighbors. A tenant may end the lease early under 47-16-17 if the landlord fails to make repairs within a reasonable time after a request, and a landlord may end it under 47-16-16 if the tenant uses the property contrary to the agreement.

The Attorney General's office does not take complaints about landlord and tenant disputes or mediate them. Tenants can turn to Legal Services of North Dakota, a private attorney or small claims court, and discrimination complaints go to the North Dakota Department of Labor.

How eviction works

Evicting a tenant is a court action here, and nothing short of a district court order lets a landlord remove one. The grounds are listed in N.D.C.C. 47-32-01, and the main ones for a rental follow.

  • Holding over after the lease ends, or failing to pay rent within three days after it is due.
  • Unreasonably disturbing other tenants' peaceful enjoyment.
  • Materially violating the written lease.
  • Remaining after a foreclosure sale, deed or cancelled contract for deed once the redemption time has expired.

Before filing a holdover, nonpayment, foreclosure-related or lease-violation case, the landlord first serves three days' written notice of intent to evict. The court summons sets an appearance date between 3 and 15 days after it is issued. If the landlord wins, the judgment is for immediate restitution of the premises, although the court may stay enforcement up to five days when immediate removal would cause substantial hardship.

A landlord may not lock a tenant out, cut off utilities or take belongings. If an LLC or corporation owns the property, the court's published self-help forms cannot be used, and the entity must be represented by a lawyer admitted in North Dakota.

Eviction records and unpaid rent

A claim for accrued rent and damages can be joined with the eviction action, but other claims generally cannot, and a tenant's counterclaims are limited to setoffs against rent or damages. Section 47-32-05 lets a person move to seal an eviction record for nonpayment or property damage seven years after the order is satisfied, if there has been no other eviction in that time.

Back rent and damages are tied to the landlord's own claim against the tenant, so a landlord who sells should settle in the sale contract who keeps the right to collect them.

Checklist before selling a rental

A short checklist keeps a rental sale clean.

  • Pull the lease, the move-in condition statement and the deposit records.
  • Confirm the deposit is in a federally insured, interest-bearing account and decide how it will transfer.
  • Give written notice before every showing and ask for a specific time.
  • If the buyer wants the house vacant, use the notice rules for the tenancy type, and file for eviction only on a statutory ground.
  • Keep rent payment methods open: a landlord may not charge a fee for accepting cash, a check or a money order for rent.

Tell any buyer up front whether the tenant will stay, because that decides which notice rules apply and how long the process takes. A cash buyer who takes the house with the tenant in place can spare you the notice periods, but the deposit still has to be accounted for at closing.

Frequently asked questions

How much can a landlord charge for a security deposit?

A landlord can generally charge up to one month's rent. Higher limits apply to a tenant with a felony conviction or a prior judgment for violating a rental agreement, and pet deposits are capped separately at the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent.

How long does a landlord have to return a deposit?

Thirty days. Deductions must be itemized in writing, and the balance goes back to the tenant, within 30 days after the lease ends and the tenant gives up possession.

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy?

At least one calendar month's written notice, from either the landlord or the tenant, given at any time.

Can a landlord show the house to buyers while it is rented?

Yes, within reason. Entry for showings must be at reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner, and the landlord must notify the tenant and seek consent for a specific time unless that is impractical.

Can a landlord evict a tenant without going to court?

No. A tenant cannot be evicted without a court order from a North Dakota district court, and lockouts, utility shutoffs and taking belongings are not allowed.
